> This vignette belongs to an **unofficial**, refactored distribution of
> iCARE. The official package is distributed by
> [Bioconductor](https://bioconductor.org/packages/iCARE/). The interface
> is the same; `vignette("differences", package = "iCARE")` lists every
> difference.

## What iCARE does

iCARE (*Individualized Coherent Absolute Risk Estimation*) estimates the
**absolute risk** of a disease: the probability that a person who is free of
the disease at age $a$ develops it before age $a + \tau$, allowing for the
possibility of dying of another cause first. A relative risk ("women with
this profile have 1.5 times the average risk") is hard to act on; an absolute
risk ("a 4.2% chance of breast cancer in the next 10 years") is what
screening and prevention guidelines use.

An iCARE model is assembled from components that are usually estimated in
different studies:

| Component | Arguments | Typical source |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Relative risks of the risk factors | `model.formula`, `model.cov.info`, `model.log.RR`; `model.snp.info` for SNPs | cohort or case-control studies, genome-wide association studies |
| Distribution of the risk factors in the population | `model.ref.dataset` (and `model.ref.dataset.weights`) | a survey representative of the population |
| Age-specific incidence of the disease | `model.disease.incidence.rates` | a cancer registry, e.g. SEER |
| Age-specific mortality from other causes | `model.competing.incidence.rates` | national vital statistics |

The hazard of the disease at age $t$ for a person with risk factors $z$ is
$\lambda(t \mid z) = \lambda_0(t) \exp\{\beta' x(z)\}$, where $x(z)$ is the
design-matrix row that `model.formula` makes from $z$ and $\beta$ are the log
relative risks. The baseline hazard $\lambda_0$ is not supplied: iCARE
calibrates it so that the average hazard of the people still free of the
disease at each age, in the reference population, equals the population's
incidence rate. This is what makes the model *coherent*: averaged over the
population, it reproduces the incidence it was built from. The absolute risk
over $[a, a + \tau)$ then accounts for the competing mortality $m(t)$:

$$
AR(a, \tau \mid z) = \int_a^{a+\tau} \lambda(t \mid z)
  \exp\left\{-\int_a^t \big(\lambda(u \mid z) + m(u)\big)\, du\right\} dt,
$$

computed, as in all versions of iCARE, with rates that are constant within
each year of age.

## The example data

The package includes the inputs of a breast cancer risk model (13 classical
risk factors and 72 SNPs), the incidence and mortality rates of US women, a
reference dataset, three women to apply the model to, and two simulated
validation studies. `?bc_data` describes each object.

```{r data}
library(iCARE)
data("bc_data", package = "iCARE")

bc_model_formula
head(ref_cov_dat, 3)
bc_inc[bc_inc[, 1] %in% seq(40, 80, by = 10), ]   # age, annual incidence rate
```

## A model with classical risk factors

The 30-year risk, from age 50 to 80, of the three example women:

```{r risk-factors}
risk_factors <- computeAbsoluteRisk(
  model.formula = bc_model_formula,
  model.cov.info = bc_model_cov_info,
  model.log.RR = bc_model_log_or,
  model.ref.dataset = ref_cov_dat,
  model.disease.incidence.rates = bc_inc,
  model.competing.incidence.rates = mort_inc,
  apply.age.start = 50,
  apply.age.interval.length = 30,
  apply.cov.profile = new_cov_prof,
  return.refs.risk = TRUE
)
risk_factors
```

The result is a list:

* `risk`: the absolute risks, one per profile;
* `details`: a data frame with each profile's interval, risk and risk
  factors;
* `beta.used`: the log relative risks used;
* `refs.risk`: the risks of the women in the reference dataset over the same
  interval (because `return.refs.risk = TRUE`), which show where a profile
  falls in the population;
* `lps`: the linear predictors $\beta' x(z)$, with `return.lp = TRUE`.

```{r details}
columns <- c("Int_Start", "Int_End", "Risk_Estimate", "famhist", "bmi_dec")
risk_factors$details[, columns]
summary(risk_factors$refs.risk)
```

The three women against the population distribution of risk:

```{r population-figure, fig.alt = "Density of the 30-year risks of the reference population, with the risks of the three women marked."}
library(ggplot2)
women <- data.frame(risk = 100 * risk_factors$risk[, 1], label = 1:3)
ggplot(data.frame(risk = 100 * risk_factors$refs.risk), aes(risk)) +
  geom_density(fill = "grey88", colour = "grey35") +
  geom_vline(data = women, aes(xintercept = risk), colour = "#B2182B",
             linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_text(data = women, aes(x = risk, y = Inf, label = label),
            hjust = -0.6, vjust = 1.5, size = 3.6, colour = "#B2182B") +
  labs(x = "Absolute risk of breast cancer from age 50 to 80 (%)",
       y = "Density",
       title = "The three women in the population distribution of risk",
       caption = "Lines: the risks of women 1, 2 and 3") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

`plot()` of a result draws the distribution of the profiles' risks, which
is useful when the profiles are many (a cohort, or the reference population
itself).

### Describing the relative-risk model

`model.cov.info` has one element per risk factor of `model.formula`: its
`name`, its `type` (`"continuous"` or `"factor"`) and, for a factor, all its
`levels` and optionally its referent level `ref`.

```{r cov-info}
str(bc_model_cov_info[[3]])
```

`model.log.RR` holds one log relative risk per column of the design matrix
that the formula makes from the reference dataset, named like those columns
(any order). To see the names a formula makes:

```{r design-columns}
design_columns <- colnames(model.matrix(bc_model_formula,
                                        cbind(diagnosis = 0, ref_cov_dat)))[-1]
head(design_columns)
all(design_columns %in% names(bc_model_log_or))
```

A missing or extra name stops with a message that lists the expected names.

### Incidence and mortality rates

Rates are annual rates by single year of age (a two-column table: age,
rate) or by age band (three columns: first age, last age, rate). They must
cover every year of age in the risk intervals; a gap is reported with the
ages concerned. `model.competing.incidence.rates = NULL` ignores competing
mortality, which overstates risks at older ages.

The calibrated baseline hazard is kept with the result, with the mean
relative risk of the women still free of breast cancer at each age:

```{r calibration}
calibration <- attr(risk_factors, "calibration")
calibration[calibration$age %in% seq(40, 80, by = 10), ]
```

## Missing risk factors

Profiles may have missing risk factors (`NA`). For a profile with observed risk factors $z_o$ and missing ones $Z_m$, iCARE
estimates $E[AR(z_o, Z_m) \mid z_o]$, the risk averaged over the
distribution of the missing risk factors in people like her. The reference
population is divided into 100 groups (percentiles) of the linear predictor
of the observed risk factors; the woman's own observed risk factors are
completed with the missing values of each reference person in her group, and
the risks of these completed profiles are averaged with the reference
weights. Interactions between an observed and a missing risk factor are
evaluated on the completed profiles. A profile with no observed risk factor
gets the average risk of the population.

For example, the first woman, with and without her body mass index:

```{r missing-bmi}
woman <- new_cov_prof[c(1, 1), ]
woman$bmi_dec[2] <- NA
completed <- computeAbsoluteRisk(
  model.formula = bc_model_formula, model.cov.info = bc_model_cov_info,
  model.log.RR = bc_model_log_or, model.ref.dataset = ref_cov_dat,
  model.disease.incidence.rates = bc_inc,
  model.competing.incidence.rates = mort_inc,
  apply.age.start = 50, apply.age.interval.length = 30,
  apply.cov.profile = woman
)
data.frame(bmi_dec = woman$bmi_dec, risk = completed$risk[, 1])
```

## Adding SNPs

A polygenic component is added with `model.snp.info`: each SNP's name,
per-allele odds ratio and risk-allele frequency.

```{r snps}
head(bc_72_snps, 3)
```

iCARE simulates the genotypes of the reference population under
Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (`n.imp` independent sets, 5 by default). With
`model.bin.fh.name`, the genotypes are simulated given each person's family
history, and the family-history log relative risk is attenuated by half the
variance of the polygenic score, because family history partly reflects the
same genes. Because the genotypes are simulated, results depend on the
random number generator: set the seed for reproducible results.

```{r risk-snps}
set.seed(50)
risk_snps <- computeAbsoluteRisk(
  model.formula = bc_model_formula,
  model.cov.info = bc_model_cov_info,
  model.snp.info = bc_72_snps,
  model.log.RR = bc_model_log_or,
  model.ref.dataset = ref_cov_dat,
  model.disease.incidence.rates = bc_inc,
  model.competing.incidence.rates = mort_inc,
  model.bin.fh.name = "famhist",
  apply.age.start = 50,
  apply.age.interval.length = 30,
  apply.cov.profile = new_cov_prof,
  apply.snp.profile = new_snp_prof
)
cbind(risk_factors = risk_factors$risk[, 1], with_snps = risk_snps$risk[, 1])
```

Missing genotypes (`NA` in `apply.snp.profile`) are handled like missing
risk factors; the first two women above have 5 and 6 missing genotypes.
Without `apply.snp.profile`, all SNPs are treated as missing.

### A SNP-only model

Leave the covariate arguments out for a model of SNPs alone. Without
genotypes, the result is the population-average risk; `refs.risk` then holds
the risks of simulated people.

```{r snp-only}
set.seed(50)
snp_only <- computeAbsoluteRisk(
  model.snp.info = bc_72_snps,
  model.disease.incidence.rates = bc_inc,
  model.competing.incidence.rates = mort_inc,
  apply.age.start = 50,
  apply.age.interval.length = 30,
  apply.snp.profile = new_snp_prof,
  return.refs.risk = TRUE
)
snp_only$risk
quantile(snp_only$refs.risk, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))
```

## Different intervals for different people

`apply.age.start` and `apply.age.interval.length` take one value for all
profiles or one per profile, and fractional ages are used exactly (the
fraction of a year of age is weighted by the time spent in it):

```{r intervals}
by_age <- computeAbsoluteRisk(
  model.formula = bc_model_formula, model.cov.info = bc_model_cov_info,
  model.log.RR = bc_model_log_or, model.ref.dataset = ref_cov_dat,
  model.disease.incidence.rates = bc_inc,
  model.competing.incidence.rates = mort_inc,
  apply.age.start = c(45, 52.5, 60),
  apply.age.interval.length = c(5, 7.5, 10),
  apply.cov.profile = new_cov_prof
)
by_age$details[, c("Int_Start", "Int_End", "Risk_Estimate")]
```

## A model that changes with age

Relative risks often differ before and after menopause.
`computeAbsoluteRiskSplitInterval()` uses one model before a cut age and
another after it. With $AR_1$ the risk before the cut age $c$, $S_1$ the
probability of reaching $c$ alive and free of the disease, and $AR_2$ the
risk from $c$ on, the risk over the whole interval is
$AR = AR_1 + S_1 \cdot AR_2$.

```{r split}
split <- computeAbsoluteRiskSplitInterval(
  model.formula = bc_model_formula,
  model.cov.info = bc_model_cov_info,
  model.log.RR = bc_model_log_or,
  model.log.RR.2 = bc_model_log_or_post_50,
  model.ref.dataset = ref_cov_dat,
  model.ref.dataset.2 = ref_cov_dat_post_50,
  model.disease.incidence.rates = bc_inc,
  model.competing.incidence.rates = mort_inc,
  apply.age.start = 40,
  apply.age.interval.length = 40,
  cut.time = 50,
  apply.cov.profile = new_cov_prof
)
split
```

Arguments ending in `.2` describe the model after the cut age; those left
out are taken from the model before it.

## Weighted reference samples

When the reference dataset is a survey sample with unequal selection
probabilities, give the survey weights in `model.ref.dataset.weights`. They
are used to calibrate the baseline hazard and to average over the reference
population for missing risk factors.
